name: Dar Fur Daju
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible
sweep_summary: darf1239 (Dar Fur Daju; Lagawa/Lagowa and Nyala are Glottolog alternate names) is not in the catalog. The only titled item, Ismail 2007 'Noun Classes in Daju Lagawa and the Role of Stress' (Köppe, Nilo-Saharan 22: 115-122), is about this language (Glottolog links it to [daj]) but could not be opened: no open copy anywhere reachable, publisher PDF for purchase, Harvard print (WID Offsite PL8026.N49 N54 2001) -> HIGH priority to acquire. Second-hand, the JALL 30 (2009: 107) review calls it a number-marking taxonomy, and Dimmendaal 2015 (The Leopard's Spots, ch. 3, pp. 32-33; Brill, paywalled) reports from his own unpublished data that Nuba-Mountains Daju 'appear to have tonal accent' with 'one prominent high peak (involving pitch rather than intensity) per word in most cases', explicitly disputing Ismail's stress claim; Alamin Mubarak 2006/2013a's stress analysis concerns Laggori (a different Daju language). Both Ismail 2007 and Dimmendaal 2015 pp. 32-33 are the pages to get; neither snippet gives a placement rule. On-disk material (Aviles 2008: initial stress in Dar Daju Daju of Chad, dard1243; Boyeldieu 2009: Lagowa data unmarked for tone/stress) does not describe darf1239 stress. Google/Bing/DDG/Mojeek/Brave, Brill, SIL, HathiTrust, archive.org search, Ulster PURE, khartoumspace, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, CORE all gated or rate-limited. Saved: ( updated).

new_statements.quote: Daju languages spoken in the Nuba Mountains appear to have tonal accent (as do Cushitic languages like Somali). Ismail (2007) argues that there is stress in Daju of Lagowa, a claim that does not tally with my own unpublished data. According to my data, there appears to be one prominent high peak (involving pitch rather than intensity) per word in most cases.
new_statements.citation: Dimmendaal, Gerrit J. (2015). The Leopard's Spots: Essays on Language, Cognition and Culture. Leiden: Brill. Ch. 3, pp. 25-63 (DOI 10.1163/9789004224148_004).
new_statements.locator: pp. 32-33 (Google Books search-inside page numbers; full text not opened, reconstructed from snippets)
new_statements.reading: First-hand (own field data) but snippet-level: Lagowa Daju (darf1239) is claimed to have a pitch-accent/tonal-accent system with one prominent high pitch peak per word, contradicting Ismail 2007's stress analysis; the position of the peak is not stated in the recovered text, and the author himself flags the analysis as needing a proper phonetic study. Not a stress-placement statement; it is a prosodic-type statement (pitch accent, not intensity stress) that any future catalog coding for darf1239 must weigh against Ismail 2007 pp. 115-122.

sources.quote: Daju languages spoken in the Nuba Mountains appear to have tonal accent (as do Cushitic languages like Somali). Ismail (2007) argues that there is stress in Daju of Lagowa, a claim that does not tally with my own unpublished data. According to my data, there appears to be one prominent high peak (involving pitch rather than intensity) per word in most cases. [...] Daju of Lagowa. Alamin Mubarak (2006, 2013a) describes Daju of Laggori as a language with stress rather than pitch accent or tonal distinctions. Although this possibility cannot be excluded, a more detailed phonetic and phonological investigation of the prosodic system would seem to be in order.
sources.note: First-hand (author's own unpublished field data): disputes Ismail 2007's stress analysis of Lagowa Daju; describes the word prosody as tonal/pitch accent with one prominent high pitch peak per word in most cases; does not state the position of the peak; calls for a fuller phonetic study. Reconstructed from six Google Books snippets (feeds API + SearchWithinVolume2), full text not opened.
